newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Disappointed Swiss Jews pin hopes on Volcker panel.
newsitem.headline: Disappointed Swiss Jews pin hopes on Volcker panel.

text.p: Swiss Jews, disappointed that banks have linked only a fraction of the dormant wealth they hold to Nazi Holocaust victims, were pinning their hopes on Wednesday on a high-powered independent auditing panel.

Swiss banking ombudsman Hanspeter Haeni said on Wednesday the hunt for unclaimed wealth in secretive Swiss banks' vaults had found valid claims for 1.6 million francs ($1.26 million), of which only 11,000 francs ($8,690) was held by Jews.
"We were a bit disappointed," said Thomas Lyssy, vice president of the Swiss Federation of Jewish Communities. "We expected a little bit more money to be given to heirs of Holocaust victims."

Lyssy's reaction was mild compared with that of the World Jewish Congress, whose vice president, Kalman Sultanik, called Haeni's probe "pathetic" and said he was "acting as a photo copying service for the Swiss banks".

The work of checking that banks are acting honestly in the emotion-charged search now falls to a commission agreed in May by Jewish groups and the Swiss Bankers Association and headed by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker.
Jewish representaitves and Swiss bankers each have three people on the panel, which is expected to announce within days the auditors it has chosen to pore over banks' wartime records.
"I think it is important that the Volcker Commission controls and checks all that work (by the banks)," Lyssy said in an interview.

He said it was not that the Jewish community did not trust the banking ombudsman who was named by banks as the first stop for people eager to find out if they still were owed money left by dead relatives in Swiss banks.

"I am sure Haeni himself is an honest man, but nobody has been checking the work of the banks up until now. This will change when the Volcker Commission has the audit firm and they start work," he said.
"I think the Volcker Commission has a lot of work to do. A lot of expectations await them."
Swiss commentators took widely different lines in intrepeting Haeni's interim report.

The liberal Tages-Anzeiger daily had a front-page cartoon showing a Swiss banker tossing a few coins from a fortress -- its drawbridge firmly closed -- to people below carrying a battering ram and holding a sign reading "dormant wealth".
"You should be satisfied now," he is shouting.

But the conservative Neue Zuercher Zeitung said it was in line with expectations and indicated few heirs would be found for the 38.7 million francs ($30.7 million) banks say remain in dormant accounts of all kinds, not just those opened by Jews.
"The obvious thing to do would be to give this money to people who were close to the victims," it commented.

"But there were many victims of the Nazis, mainly Jews, but also Gypsies, communists, homosexuals, the mentally handicapped and avowed Christians, people who had to die for reasons that can hardly be imagined today," it said.
"A dignified decision should be promoted that clearly rises above the spirit of reproaching Switzerland that has been seen for months," it added.
Lyssy agreed the discussion was moving in this direction.
"I think this will be the issue at the end," he said.
